<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_document">Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures<span class="ltx_pubnotes"><span class="ltx_pubnotes_content"><span class="ltx_pubnote ltx_role_thanks"><span class="ltx_note_name">Thanks: </span><span id="id1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:70%;">We are grateful to Lin William Cong, Urban Jermann, Shimon Kogan, Tim Roughgarden, Adrien Verdelhan, as well as conference participants at the 2024 Utah Winter Finance Conference and seminar participants at a16z Crypto, Hebrew University, Reichman University, and the Virtual Derivatives Workshop for their insightful feedback and helpful comments.
Songrun He is at Washington University in St. Louis (<a href="mailto:h.songrun@wustl.edu" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_medium">h.songrun@wustl.edu</a>). Asaf Manela is at Washington University in St. Louis and Reichman University (<a href="mailto:amanela@wustl.edu" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_medium">amanela@wustl.edu</a>). Omri Ross is at University of Copenhagen (<a href="mailto:omri@di.ku.dk" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_medium">omri@di.ku.dk</a>), and Chief Blockchain Scientist at the eToro Group. Victor von Wachter is at University of Copenhagen (<a href="mailto:victor.vonwachter@di.ku.dk" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_medium">victor.vonwachter@di.ku.dk</a>).</span></span></span></span></h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Songrun He
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Asaf Manela
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Omri Ross
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Victor von Wachter
</span></span></div>
<div class="ltx_dates">First draft December 2022. This draft June 2024.</div>

<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Abstract</span></p>
</div>
<div id="p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="p2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Perpetual futures—swap contracts that never expire—are the most popular derivative traded in cryptocurrency markets, with more than $100 billion traded daily.
Perpetuals provide investors with leveraged exposure to cryptocurrencies, which does not require rollover or direct cryptocurrency holding.
To keep the gap between perpetual futures and spot prices small, long position holders periodically pay short position holders a funding rate proportional to this gap. The funding rate incentivizes trades that tend to narrow the futures-spot gap.
But unlike fixed-maturity futures, perpetuals are not guaranteed to converge to the spot price of their underlying asset at any time, and familiar no-arbitrage prices for perpetuals are not available, as the contracts have no expiry date to enforce arbitrage.
Here, using a weaker notion of random-maturity arbitrage, we derive no-arbitrage prices for perpetual futures in frictionless markets and no-arbitrage bounds for markets with trading costs.
These no-arbitrage prices provide a valuable benchmark for perpetual futures and simultaneously prescribe a strategy to exploit divergence from these fundamental values.
Empirically, we find that deviations of crypto perpetual futures from no-arbitrage prices are considerably larger than those documented in traditional currency markets. These deviations comove across cryptocurrencies and diminish over time as crypto markets develop and become more efficient. A simple trading strategy generates large Sharpe ratios even for investors paying the highest trading costs on Binance, which is currently the largest crypto exchange by volume.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">JEL Classification</span>: G11, G12, G13 
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Keywords</span>: Perpetual futures, crypto, random-maturity arbitrage, funding rate</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Perpetual futures are, by far, the most popular derivative traded in cryptocurrency markets, generating a daily volume of more than $100 billion.
Prior to the recent collapse of FTX, perpetual futures were among the most actively traded products on the exchange, with the now-bankrupt hedge fund Alameda Research taking the other side of many such leveraged trades. Despite their central role in crypto markets, there is relatively little work studying these derivatives. In this paper we ask: what are the theoretical fundamental values of perpetual futures, and how large are deviations from these fundamentals empirically?</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Perpetuals are derivatives that allow investors to speculate on or hedge against cryptocurrency price fluctuations using high leverage, without needing to acquire the cryptocurrencies or to roll them over.
Like traditional fixed-maturity futures, at initiation, a long and short counterparty agree on an initial futures price without exchanging any money, other than posting margin with the exchange. Both parties can enter or exit the contract at any time, with profits or losses continuously calculated and allocated to each side’s margin account based on prevailing market prices.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Unlike fixed-maturity futures, perpetuals do not expire. This feature enhances the liquidity of the contract, as there is no staggering of contracts with different maturities traded on the exchange, and only a single perpetual futures contract per underlying asset is listed. Moreover, this instrument does not require market participants to roll over their futures positions and is traded 24/7.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Because they have no set expiration date, perpetuals are not guaranteed to converge to the spot price of their underlying asset at any given time, and the usual no-arbitrage prices for perpetuals are not applicable.
To minimize the gap between perpetual futures and spot prices, long position holders periodically pay short position holders a ’funding rate’ proportional to this gap to incentivize trades that narrow it.
For example, when the futures price exceeds the spot price, arbitrageurs who borrow cash to long the spot and simultaneously short the futures would receive the funding rate. Their trades would tend to increase the spot price and decrease the futures price.
A narrow gap means that perpetual futures offer effective exposure to variation in the spot price of the underlying asset to hedging and speculating investors. Typically, the funding rate is paid every eight hours and approximately equals the average futures-spot spread over the preceding eight hours.
Note that the strategy just sketched, commonly referred to as ’funding rate arbitrage,’ is not risk-free even disregarding margin requirements and trading costs, simply because there is no predetermined expiration date when the trade would be unwound at a profit.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We derive no-arbitrage prices for perpetual futures in frictionless markets and derive no-arbitrage bounds in markets with trading costs.
The theoretical perpetual futures price is proportional to the spot price of the underlying, with a constant of proportionality that increases in the ratio of the interest rate to a constant that determines the magnitude of the funding rate. The interest rate captures the cost of borrowing cash to finance holding the underlying, while the funding rate captures the benefit of shorting the futures.
Thus, intuitively, the future-spot spread is larger when the cash borrowing interest rate is large relative to the funding rate.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Our derivation relies on a weaker notion of arbitrage that we call <em id="S1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">random-maturity arbitrage</em>. As its name suggests, unlike traditional riskless arbitrage, we allow the strategy’s time-to-maturity to be random. At first glance, one might object that such prices are not truly based on riskless arbitrage. Note, however, that riskless no-arbitrage pricing is usually just a useful fiction <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pedersen, 2019</a>)</cite>. For example, in real-world futures markets, arbitrageurs must maintain a margin account during the entire period in which the arbitrage trade is open. Temporary worsening of apparent arbitrage opportunities can lead to liquidations and losses. As the saying goes, an arbitrageur must remain liquid longer than the market stays irrational. Thus, even arbitrage opportunities that appear to be riskless in theory, may be risky in practice.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Our no-arbitrage prices provide a useful benchmark for perpetual futures and simultaneously prescribe a strategy to exploit divergence from these fundamental values.
Motivated by the theoretical understanding, we study the empirical deviations of the perpetual futures price from the spot.
We find that the mean deviation from our benchmark is modest and statistically insignificant, which suggests that it is a useful benchmark for futures prices.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Around this benchmark, however, perpetual futures often differ significantly from spot prices.
The mean <em id="S1.p8.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">absolute</em> deviation is about 60% to 90% per year across different cryptocurrencies, which is considerably larger than the deviations documented in traditional currency markets by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du, Tepper, and Verdelhan (2018)</a></cite>.
We find strong comovement of the futures-spot gap across different cryptocurrencies. This comovement can be due to commonality in funding and market liquidity faced by arbitrageurs who operate in multiple cryptocurrencies. Common sentiment could also drive the difference in futures demand relative to the spot. Overall, the deviation’s magnitude is comparable to our theoretic no-arbitrage bound calibrated to actual trading fees.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p9.1" class="ltx_p">Deviations decline on average about 11% a year, consistent with an increase in arbitrage capital and competition among arbitrageurs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kondor, 2009</a>)</cite>. The narrowing gap provides an additional perspective on the downfall of Alameda Research and Three Arrows Capital. According to news reports and interviews, both hedge funds seem to have pivoted from such arbitrage activity around late 2021 to early 2022 and started taking more directional bets on cryptocurrencies, with both direct unhedged crypto holdings and investments in crypto startups. The large declines in crypto prices in 2022 subsequently exhausted their capital and led to their bankruptcies.<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
            
            
            
          See, for example, Forbes, November 19, 2022, on <a href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/jeffkauflin/2022/11/19/how-did-sam-bankman-frieds-alameda-research-lose-so-much-money" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">How Did Sam Bankman-Fried’s Alameda Research Lose So Much Money?</a>, Odd Lots, November 17, 2022, on <a href="https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2022-11-17/odd-lots-podcast-understanding-sam-bankman-fried-s-ftx-crypto-collapse" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">Understanding the Collapse of Sam Bankman-Fried’s Crypto Empire</a>, and Hugh Hendry’s interview on December 3, 2022 of Kyle Davies on the <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TzGdkB0xbCE" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">Collapse of Three Arrows Capital</a>.</span></span></span></p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p10.1" class="ltx_p">To understand the economics of the futures-spot spread, we consider a trading strategy motivated by the random-maturity arbitrage theory. Whenever the futures-spot spread exceeds the theoretical bound under certain trading cost tiers, we open the trading position and close it when the futures-spot spread returns to its theoretical relationship under no trading costs. We find that empirically, the random maturity arbitrage strategy generates a sizable Sharpe ratio even under high trading costs. For example, for Bitcoin perpetual futures, the strategy generates a Sharpe ratio of 1.8 under high trading costs typical of retail investors, and up to 3.5 for highly-active market makers who pay no such fees. The strategy’s performance is even better for Ether and other cryptocurrencies and delivers significant alphas relative to the 3-factor model of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu, Tsyvinski, and Wu (2022)</a></cite> and the 5-factor model of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cong, Karolyi, Tang, and Zhao (2022b)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p11.1" class="ltx_p">The strong performance of our simple trading strategy, which exploits deviations from the random-maturity no-arbitrage bounds we derive, provides compelling evidence for the usefulness of these bounds as a benchmark for perpetual futures prices. The strategy generates high Sharpe ratios, even for investors subject to the highest trading costs on Binance. This indicates that the no-arbitrage prices serve as an effective anchor for perpetual futures, with profitable random maturity arbitrage opportunities arising when market prices diverge significantly from these fundamental values. Thus, the success of the trading strategy underscores the practical value and validity of our theoretical no-arbitrage results.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p12" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p12.1" class="ltx_p">What explains these large no-arbitrage deviations?
One natural explanation is that liquidity in crypto markets is insufficient for arbitrageurs to eliminate such violations. Our finding that the spreads decline over time is consistent with liquidity improving as these markets develop, and leaves open the possibility that they will narrow going forward.
We also find, however, that past return momentum significantly explains the futures-spot gap with a time-series regression <math id="S1.p12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> of more than <math id="S1.p12.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50\%</annotation></semantics></math>. When past returns are high, futures tend to trade at a higher price relative to the spot. This indicates positive feedback or momentum trading behavior in the perpetual futures market. This correlation may linger even as crypto markets become more efficient.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p13" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p13.1" class="ltx_p">The existing literature on perpetual futures mainly focuses on empirical evidence. See e.g. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Alexander, Choi, Park, and Sohn (2020)</a></cite>, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">De Blasis and Webb (2022)</a></cite>, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ferko, Moin, Onur, and Penick (2022)</a></cite>, and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Streltsov and Ruan (2022)</a></cite>. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Angeris, Chitra, Evans, and Lorig (2022)</a></cite> provide a theoretical no-arbitrage analysis of perpetuals, but they make over-simplifying assumptions by assuming the payoff from the perpetual is a fixed function of the underlying spot price. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Christin, Routledge, Soska, and Zetlin-Jones (2022)</a></cite> present a novel study on the strategy of longing the spot and shorting the perpetual futures to understand the demand pressure in the market. They document a significant return to this trading strategy and attribute the profits to differences of opinion and leverage constraints in the market. Our paper provides a general explanation for their findings as perpetual futures are more expensive relative to the theoretical no-arbitrage price for most of the recent sample period across major cryptocurrencies. Therefore, longing the spot and shorting the futures would be consistent with arbitrage trading directions. Overall, compared to the existing literature, we illustrate the fundamental mechanism behind the perpetual design and derive theoretical no-arbitrage prices and bounds for this instrument.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p14" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p14.1" class="ltx_p">Also related is recent literature on fixed maturity futures in the crypto space. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schmeling, Schrimpf, and Todorov (2022)</a></cite> provide a comprehensive analysis of the carry of fixed-maturity crypto futures, with the carry defined following the general definition of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koijen, Moskowitz, Pedersen, and Vrugt (2018)</a></cite>. They document volatile convenience yields for fixed-maturity crypto futures and attribute this to trend-chasing small investors and the relative scarcity of arbitrage capital. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cong, He, and Tang (2022a)</a></cite> provide a novel link of the volatile convenience yield to the staking, service flow, and transaction convenience of the underlying tokens. They show that the large deviation from uncovered interest rate parity can be reconciled with transaction convenience. Our paper focuses on perpetual futures rather than fixed maturity futures and extends fixed-maturity to random-maturity no-arbitrage pricing.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p15" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p15.1" class="ltx_p">More broadly, our paper contributes to the understanding of the frictions and arbitrage in cryptocurrency markets. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Makarov and Schoar (2020)</a></cite> study price deviations across exchanges. They find large gaps across countries, highlighting the important role played by capital controls and slow-moving arbitrage capital as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Duffie (2010)</a></cite>. Our analysis focuses on the price wedge between the spot and the futures market. We find that even within an exchange, futures prices deviate from their theoretical arbitrage-free values. These results indicate there are significant limits to arbitrage as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gromb and Vayanos (2018)</a></cite> for cryptocurrencies in the early years. Finally, our finding that deviations from the no-arbitrage benchmark in crypto markets are highly correlated across currencies suggests that a common risk factor drives this variation as documented by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lustig, Roussanov, and Verdelhan (2011)</a></cite> in traditional currency markets.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p16" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p16.1" class="ltx_p">The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Section <a href="#S2" title="2 An Introduction to Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> provides the institutional details and history of perpetual futures. Section <a href="#S3" title="3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> presents the no-arbitrage analysis of the perpetual futures market and derives the theoretical price of perpetual futures. Section <a href="#S4" title="4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> demonstrates the empirical futures-spot deviation and presents the simple theory-motivated trading strategy that can exploit the arbitrage opportunity. Section <a href="#S5" title="5 Explaining Futures-spot Deviations ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> provides some explanation for the deviation between futures and the spot. Section <a href="#S6" title="6 Conclusion ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> concludes.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>An Introduction to Perpetual Futures</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The idea of perpetual futures was first introduced by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shiller (1993)</a></cite>. The goal was to set up a perpetual claim on the cash flows of an illiquid asset. For example, the underlying illiquid asset could be a house that generates rents as cash flows. The purpose of the perpetual futures is to enable price discovery for the underlying with an illiquid or hard-to-measure price. Perpetual futures have no expiration date but cash is exchanged between the long and the short side: after buying the perpetual futures, the long side is entitled to receive the flow cash flow from the short side and they settle the price difference when exiting the position.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F1" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2212.06888v5/figures/exchange_volume.png" id="S2.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/184;" width="476" height="184" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Total trading volumes of perpetual futures across exchanges</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S2.F1.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="S2.F1.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">The figure displays the 7-day moving average daily traded volume for perpetual futures across all exchanges in blue. The median daily volume is $17.8 bn. (2020), $132.0 bn. (2021) and $101.9 bn. (2022). This translates to a yearly volume of $8,551 bn. (2020), $51,989 bn. (2021) and $39,306 bn. (2022) respectively. Additionally, the grey line depicts the ratio between the traded volume in perpetuals and spot markets. In 2022 the Perpetual markets are consistently trading between 2x or 3.5x the spot volume. The data is obtained from CoinGecko, a crypto data specialist. We exclude exchanges that are known for misrepresenting data (e.g. forms of wash trading).</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Perpetual futures in crypto markets similarly have no expiration date and cash is exchanged between the long and the short side, but their purpose is different from Shiller’s original idea. First, unlike, e.g. real estate market, crypto has no inherent dividend or cash flow. Second, the price discovery argument of Shiller is most applicable to settings where spot prices are difficult to measure. Crypto spot prices, however, can be measured from active trading on different exchanges, and decentralized exchanges such as Bancor <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hertzog et al., 2017</a>)</cite> or Uniswap <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Adams et al., 2021</a>)</cite> offer price discovery for assets with minimal liquidity. The major role perpetual futures play in the crypto space is to offer an effective leveraged trading vehicle to hedge or speculate the underlying spot price movement, which makes the market more complete. It also serves as an effective tax payment optimization tool for investors.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Crypto perpetual futures were first introduced by BitMEX in 2016, which has gained great popularity in the crypto space since its inception. It initially served as an effective hedging tool for crypto miners. It was later adopted by crypto speculators interested in leveraged exposure. Nowadays, based on data from CoinGecko, the median total daily trading volume of perpetual futures across all exchanges is 101.9 billion in the year 2022 which is about <math id="S2.p3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="2\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\times</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S2.p3.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="3\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3\times</annotation></semantics></math> the total spot trading volume across these exchanges. Figure <a href="#S2.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 2 An Introduction to Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> presents the 7-day moving average of the total trading volume of perpetual futures across all exchanges. We see a significant rise in trading of perpetual futures around January 2021 and the total volume stabilizes at a level above $100 billion per day following the rise.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cong, Li, Tang, and Yang (2022c)</a></cite> document significant wash trading behavior among crypto exchanges because of competition, the ranking mechanism, and lack of regulation. They estimate that over 70% of crypto trading volume is not real. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Amiram, Lyandres, and Rabetti (2021)</a></cite> confirm this conclusion using new data and an extended methodology. Therefore, in calculating trading volume, we exclude exchanges that are known to misrepresent data.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F2" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2212.06888v5/figures/exchanges_fr_bitcoin.png" id="S2.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/192;" width="476" height="192" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Bitcoin annualized funding rate across exchanges</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S2.F2.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="S2.F2.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">The figure presents the 7-day moving average annualized funding rate for Bitcoin (BTC) across exchanges. The data is obtained from Glassnode, an analytics platform. The data covers two major market turbulences: the COVID stock market crash from February to April 2020 and the FTX insolvency in November 2022. The FTX collapse led to significant negative funding rates on all solvent exchanges. Thus, the perpetual future prices were lower than the spot prices on the solvent exchanges. Vice versa on the insolvent FTX. The funding rates become more volatile after the event, indicating increased uncertainty for the market participants.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">A key feature of crypto perpetual futures is the funding rate, which is the cash exchanged between the long and short counterparties. Its goal is to keep the futures price close to the underlying spot so that the futures can be an effective hedging tool for spot price movement. The funding rate is typically paid every 8 hours. Its value is approximately a weighted average of the prior 8 hours’ price gap of the futures and the spot. If the futures price is above the spot, the funding rate will be positive, meaning the long side of the futures needs to pay the short side. This incentivizes traders to short the futures, and in doing so, to move its price back in line with the spot. On the other hand, when the futures price is below the spot, the funding rate turns negative, which means the short side needs to pay the long side. Therefore, the funding rate is the key mechanism keeping the futures price close to the spot price.<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
            
            
            
          <a href="https://www.binance.com/en/support/faq/360033525031" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://www.binance.com/en/support/faq/360033525031</a> provides a detailed explanation of how the funding rate is calculated. We summarize the mechanism in Appendix B.</span></span></span> Note that perpetual futures cannot be replicated by rolling over 8-hour maturity futures. For the latter, every 8 hours, the price is guaranteed to converge to the underlying spot, while for the perpetual futures this is not the case.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S2.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 2 An Introduction to Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> presents the annualized 7-day moving average of Bitcoin perpetual funding rates across leading exchanges from January 2020 to December 2022.
The funding rate is positive when the futures-to-spot spread is positive, and negative otherwise. Funding rates tend to be similar across exchanges due to cross-exchange arbitrage activity, but can diverge during extreme liquidity episodes. During March 2020, as COVID-19 started to spread and liquidity evaporated, funding rates turned substantially negative in most exchanges. Funding rates turned highly positive during the crypto bull run of early 2021. The last episode highlighted is the collapse of FTX, which was the 4th largest crypto exchange at the time. The figure shows that Bitcoin futures prices were substantially higher than spot prices at FTX, but the opposite was true on other exchanges. This pattern is consistent with FTX investors liquidating their short futures positions quickly, either voluntarily to reduce their exposure to the failing exchange, or involuntarily as the exchange liquidated their underfunded positions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We next derive no-arbitrage prices for perpetual futures prices relative to spot prices. Unlike traditional futures, perpetual futures have no expiration date. To analyze arbitrage in this market, we extend the traditional notion of risk-free arbitrage, where arbitrageurs have a guaranteed positive payoff at a certain time in the future. We first describe the payoff structure of perpetual futures. We then introduce a generalized notion of an arbitrage opportunity with a certain positive payoff but at an uncertain future time.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_definition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition 1</span></span><span id="Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Perpetual futures)<span id="Thmtheorem1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">A perpetual futures contract with price <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{F_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{F_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}</annotation></semantics></math> written on an underlying asset with spot price <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{S_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{S_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}</annotation></semantics></math> is a swap agreement between the long and the short side. There is no cost to open the position. Once open, both the long side and the short side can terminate their position at any time <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>. To stay in the contract, both sides have to meet two requirements. (1) For each unit of the perpetual, the long and short sides must exchange an <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{s}-" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>−</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{s}-</annotation></semantics></math>adapted cash-flow <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa(F_{s}-S_{s})ds,\,s\in(0,t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa(F_{s}-S_{s})ds,\,s\in(0,t)</annotation></semantics></math>, referred to as the funding payment. <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> is a scaling parameter determining the magnitude of the funding rate relative to the price gap. If the value is positive, the long pays the short, and vice versa. (2) Both sides need to post mark-to-market margins to cover any losses in their margin accounts.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This definition is an approximation of real-world perpetual futures.<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
            
            
            
          To avoid price manipulation and volatile funding payments, Binance applies a clamp function to funding rate payments when the deviation is small. We provide a thorough discussion of the funding rate mechanism in Appendix B.</span></span></span> In most exchanges, the funding payment for perpetual futures is paid every <math id="S3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>8</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8</annotation></semantics></math> hours and approximately equals the average difference between the futures price and the spot over the <math id="S3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>8</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8</annotation></semantics></math> hours (<math id="S3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="480" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>480</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">480</annotation></semantics></math> minutes or <math id="S3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{1}{1095}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>1095</mn></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{1095}</annotation></semantics></math> years). If we measure time units in years, the cumulative funding rate payment during an 8-hour period is:</p>
<table id="S3.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\int_{t}^{t+1/1095}\kappa(F_{s}-S_{s})ds." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>1095</mn></mrow></mrow></msubsup><mrow><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\int_{t}^{t+1/1095}\kappa(F_{s}-S_{s})ds.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Consider the case when <math id="S3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{t}-S_{t}=G" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>G</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{t}-S_{t}=G</annotation></semantics></math>, which is constant over the 8-hour interval. In the real world, the funding rate payment would equal <math id="S3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>G</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G</annotation></semantics></math> while in our model, the number is <math id="S3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\kappa G}{1095}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>G</mi></mrow><mn>1095</mn></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\kappa G}{1095}</annotation></semantics></math>. To equalize the two, we have <math id="S3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa=1095" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1095</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa=1095</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The traditional notions of arbitrage typically consider a guaranteed positive payoff at a certain future date.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmtheorem2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_definition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmtheorem2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition 2</span></span><span id="Thmtheorem2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Riskless arbitrage)<span id="Thmtheorem2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmtheorem2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">A riskless arbitrage opportunity is defined with respect to a payoff <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> at a certain future time <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> and its price <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(x)</annotation></semantics></math>. If the following conditions are satisfied: (1) <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\geq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\geq 0</annotation></semantics></math> almost surely, (2) <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> with some positive probability, and (3) its price satisfies <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(x)\leq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(x)\leq 0</annotation></semantics></math>, then this payoff is an arbitrage opportunity <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cochrane, 2009</a>)</cite>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">There is no certain future time, however, when a perpetual futures expires and its price is guaranteed to converge to some fixed function of the spot price. Therefore, a generalized notion of arbitrage is required. Suppose the risk-free rate is constant. We define <em id="S3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">random-maturity arbitrage</em> opportunities as zero-cost strategies with a guaranteed positive payoff at a bounded uncertain future time. Stated formally:</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmtheorem3" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_definition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmtheorem3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition 3</span></span><span id="Thmtheorem3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Random-maturity arbitrage)<span id="Thmtheorem3.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmtheorem3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">A random-maturity arbitrage opportunity is defined with respect to a random payoff <math id="Thmtheorem3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> at a bounded future random time <math id="Thmtheorem3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\tau}&lt;\bar{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>τ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>&lt;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>T</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\tau}&lt;\bar{T}</annotation></semantics></math>, and its price <math id="Thmtheorem3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(x)</annotation></semantics></math>. If the following conditions are satisfied: (1) <math id="Thmtheorem3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\geq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\geq 0</annotation></semantics></math> almost surely, (2) <math id="Thmtheorem3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> with some positive probability, and (3) its price satisfies <math id="Thmtheorem3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(x)\leq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(x)\leq 0</annotation></semantics></math>, then this payoff is a random-maturity arbitrage opportunity.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Definition <a href="#Thmtheorem3" title="Definition 3 (Random-maturity arbitrage). ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> generalizes traditional arbitrage in the sense that there is a guaranteed positive payoff but at an uncertain future time. The following corollary specializes this definition for perpetual futures:</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmcorollary1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_corollary">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmcorollary1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Corollary 1</span></span><span id="Thmcorollary1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmcorollary1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmcorollary1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmcorollary1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">In the perpetual futures market, if a strategy (1) has <math id="Thmcorollary1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> cost at time <math id="Thmcorollary1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math>, and (2) for any price path of the futures and the spot, <math id="Thmcorollary1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{F_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{F_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Thmcorollary1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{S_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{S_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}</annotation></semantics></math>, there exists a bounded unwinding time <math id="Thmcorollary1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\tau}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>τ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\tau}</annotation></semantics></math> such that the strategy’s discounted payoff is positive, then this strategy is a random-maturity arbitrage.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We next show that when there is no random-maturity arbitrage, the futures price is a fixed constant times the spot price under the two following assumptions:</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmassumption1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_assumption">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmassumption1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Assumption 1</span></span><span id="Thmassumption1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmassumption1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmassumption1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmassumption1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">The risk-free short rate <math id="Thmassumption1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> in the cash market and the instantaneous interest rate on the underlying asset <math id="Thmassumption1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>r</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math> are constant.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="Thmassumption2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_assumption">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmassumption2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Assumption 2</span></span><span id="Thmassumption2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmassumption2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmassumption2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmassumption2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">The gap between the perpetual futures and its fundamental price is bounded:
<math id="Thmassumption2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sup_{t}\left|F_{t}(\omega)-\lambda S_{t}(\omega)\right|&lt;M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>sup</mo><mi>t</mi></msub><mrow><mo lspace="0em">|</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ω</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ω</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>|</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sup_{t}\left|F_{t}(\omega)-\lambda S_{t}(\omega)\right|&lt;M</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="Thmassumption2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\forall\,\omega" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0.337em">∀</mo><mi>ω</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\forall\,\omega</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="Thmassumption2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> is a proportionality constant implied by Equation (<a href="#S3.E1" title="In Proposition 1 (No-arbitrage price). ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>).</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="Thmassumption3" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_assumption">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmassumption3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Assumption 3</span></span><span id="Thmassumption3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmassumption3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmassumption3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmassumption3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">The funding rate is larger than the short rate in the cash market: <math id="Thmassumption3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa&gt;r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa&gt;r</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Assumption <a href="#Thmassumption1" title="Assumption 1. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> guarantees that there is no roll-over risk for the arbitrageurs. Assumption <a href="#Thmassumption2" title="Assumption 2. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> is a no-bubble condition, which says that the largest deviation of perpetual futures from its no-arbitrage price can be bounded by <math id="S3.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>. Assumption <a href="#Thmassumption3" title="Assumption 3. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> states that the design of the contract needs to guarantee that the reward for convergence trade is larger than deploying the capital to the risk-free asset. With these three assumptions, we can state our result as follows.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmproposition1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_proposition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmproposition1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proposition 1</span></span><span id="Thmproposition1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(No-arbitrage price)<span id="Thmproposition1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmproposition1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmproposition1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmproposition1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Under Assumptions <a href="#Thmassumption1" title="Assumption 1. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, <a href="#Thmassumption2" title="Assumption 2. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, and <a href="#Thmassumption3" title="Assumption 3. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, there is an absence of random-maturity arbitrage opportunities if and only if</span></p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{t}=\frac{\kappa}{\kappa-(r-r^{\prime})}S_{t}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mi>κ</mi><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{t}=\frac{\kappa}{\kappa-(r-r^{\prime})}S_{t}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.2" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="S3.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text">We first show when there are no random maturity arbitrage opportunities, the perpetual futures price must be given by Equation (<a href="#S3.E1" title="In Proposition 1 (No-arbitrage price). ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>). We establish this using the conjecture and verify approach.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p9.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p9.1.1" class="ltx_text">Firstly, conjecture that the equilibrium futures price is a linear function of the spot: <math id="S3.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{t}=\lambda S_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{t}=\lambda S_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> is the parameter to be determined. Consider the following two scenarios in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Proof. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. (1) <math id="S3.p9.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{0}&gt;\lambda S_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{0}&gt;\lambda S_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>; (2) <math id="S3.p9.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{0}&lt;\lambda S_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{0}&lt;\lambda S_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>. We show in the first case that arbitrageurs would long the spot and short the futures because this is a random-maturity arbitrage opportunity. We then show that the opposite strategy is optimal in the second case.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p10.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p10.1.1" class="ltx_text">For the payoff given in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Proof. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, it is worth noting that the mark-to-market margin requirements indicate any interim futures price changes will affect the payoff of the trader since she needs to post enough margin to cover losses or can invest the surplus in margin account in risk-free assets. Moreover, in the cash market, the trader needs to roll over the short-term debt to finance the position in the spot market. The interest paid from holding the underlying asset depends on the spot price.</span></p>
</div>

<th id="S3.T1.2.8.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row"><span id="S3.T1.2.8.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">Spot</span></th>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>Discounted payoffs to arbitrage strategies in perpetual futures and spot markets</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S3.T1.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="S3.T1.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">This table presents the costs and benefits of two arbitrage trading strategies: (1) when <math id="S3.T1.m23" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{0}&gt;\lambda S_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{0}&gt;\lambda S_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>, long <math id="S3.T1.m24" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> spot and short 1 futures; (2) when <math id="S3.T1.m25" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{0}&lt;\lambda S_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{0}&lt;\lambda S_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>, long 1 futures and short <math id="S3.T1.m26" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> spot. In the last row, the payoff from exiting the position is the discounted payoff from futures and spot price changes, proceeds from the cash market, and the funding rate.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S3.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p11.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p11.1.1" class="ltx_text">To start off, we need to fix <math id="S3.p11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math>. Given our conjecture, if <math id="S3.p11.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{t}=\lambda S_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{t}=\lambda S_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, both the first and second strategies in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Proof. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> should have <math id="S3.p11.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> payoff. This condition gives us the following equation:</span></p>
<table id="S3.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.Ex2"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\lambda=1+\frac{(r-r^{\prime})\lambda}{\kappa}\implies\lambda=\frac{\kappa}{\kappa-(r-r^{\prime})}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>λ</mi></mrow><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mstyle></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟹</mo><mi>λ</mi><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mi>κ</mi><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\lambda=1+\frac{(r-r^{\prime})\lambda}{\kappa}\implies\lambda=\frac{\kappa}{\kappa-(r-r^{\prime})}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>

</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.p12" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p12.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p12.1.1" class="ltx_text">Next, given this <math id="S3.p12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math>, we verify that the deviation shown in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Proof. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> implies the existence of random maturity arbitrage opportunities. In what follows, we denote the deviation by:</span></p>
<table id="S3.Ex3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{s}\equiv F_{s}-\frac{\kappa}{\kappa-(r-r^{\prime})}S_{s}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>≡</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><mfrac><mi>κ</mi><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{s}\equiv F_{s}-\frac{\kappa}{\kappa-(r-r^{\prime})}S_{s}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<p id="S3.p12.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p12.2.1" class="ltx_text">We can then write the payoffs of the two strategies in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Proof. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> respectively as:</span></p>
<table id="S3.EGx2" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.Ex4"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle-\int_{0}^{t}e^{-rs}du_{s}+\kappa\int_{0}^{t}e^{-rs}u_{s}ds" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mo>∫</mo></mstyle><msub><mrow></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>t</mi></msup><mi>e</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mi>d</mi><mi>u</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>κ</mi><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mo>∫</mo></mstyle><msub><mrow></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>t</mi></msup><mi>e</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mi>u</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>s</mi></msub><mi>d</mi><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle-\int_{0}^{t}e^{-rs}du_{s}+\kappa\int_{0}^{t}e^{-rs}u_{s}ds</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=-e^{-rt}u_{t}+u_{0}+(\kappa-r)\int_{0}^{t}u_{s}e^{-rs}ds," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>t</mi></msubsup></mstyle><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=-e^{-rt}u_{t}+u_{0}+(\kappa-r)\int_{0}^{t}u_{s}e^{-rs}ds,</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<tbody id="S3.Ex5"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
