</table>
<p id="S3.p12.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p12.3.1" class="ltx_text">where the equality follows from integration by parts.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p13" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p13.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p13.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Scenario 1:<span id="S3.p13.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> If <math id="S3.p13.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{0}&gt;\lambda S_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{0}&gt;\lambda S_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>, consider the first strategy of longing <math id="S3.p13.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> spot and shorting 1 futures. We want to show that for any price path of the perpetual futures and the spot, there exists a bounded future unwinding time <math id="S3.p13.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> such that the strategy’s payoff is positive, which would mean this is a random-maturity arbitrage. To prevent the arbitrageur from making a profit, the payoff must be nonpositive at all times <math id="S3.p13.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>:</span></span></p>
<table id="S3.EGx3" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.E2"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\underbrace{-e^{-rt}u_{t}}_{\text{spread at unwinding}}+\underbrace{u_{0}}_{\text{initial spread}}+\underbrace{(\kappa-r)\int_{0}^{t}u_{s}e^{-rs}ds}_{\text{funding payments}}\leq 0." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><munder><munder accentunder="true"><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="true">⏟</mo></munder><mtext>spread at unwinding</mtext></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><munder accentunder="true"><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="true">⏟</mo></munder><mtext>initial spread</mtext></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><munder accentunder="true"><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>t</mi></msubsup></mstyle><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">d</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="true">⏟</mo></munder><mtext>funding payments</mtext></munder></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\underbrace{-e^{-rt}u_{t}}_{\text{spread at unwinding}}+\underbrace{u_{0}}_{\text{initial spread}}+\underbrace{(\kappa-r)\int_{0}^{t}u_{s}e^{-rs}ds}_{\text{funding payments}}\leq 0.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p13.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p13.2.1" class="ltx_text">Consider the first time period when the deviation is positive. That is, <math id="S3.p13.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{s}&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{s}&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.p13.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s\in(0,\min\{t&gt;0,u_{t}=0\})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>min</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s\in(0,\min\{t&gt;0,u_{t}=0\})</annotation></semantics></math>. Rearrange the terms, the inequality becomes:</span></p>
<table id="S3.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e^{-rt}u_{t}\geq u_{0}+(\kappa-r)\int_{0}^{t}u_{s}e^{-rs}ds." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e^{-rt}u_{t}\geq u_{0}+(\kappa-r)\int_{0}^{t}u_{s}e^{-rs}ds.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p13.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p13.3.1" class="ltx_text">Let <math id="S3.p13.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\underline{u}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><munder accentunder="true"><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></munder><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\underline{u}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> denote a process, implicitly defined by <math id="S3.p13.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e^{-rt}\underline{u}_{t}=u_{0}+(\kappa-r)\int_{0}^{t}\underline{u}_{s}e^{-rs}ds" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><munder accentunder="true"><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></munder><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mrow><msub><munder accentunder="true"><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></munder><mi>s</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e^{-rt}\underline{u}_{t}=u_{0}+(\kappa-r)\int_{0}^{t}\underline{u}_{s}e^{-rs}ds</annotation></semantics></math>, which provides a lower bound for all processes <math id="S3.p13.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> satisfying inequality (<a href="#S3.E3" title="In Proof. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>). Solving this integral equation, we have:</span></p>
<table id="S3.Ex6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\underline{u}_{t}=e^{\kappa t}u_{0}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><munder accentunder="true"><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></munder><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\underline{u}_{t}=e^{\kappa t}u_{0}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p13.4" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p13.4.1" class="ltx_text">From the above expression, there exists a time <math id="S3.p13.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{T}=\frac{\log(M)-\log(u_{0})}{\kappa}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>T</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{T}=\frac{\log(M)-\log(u_{0})}{\kappa}</annotation></semantics></math>, such that <math id="S3.p13.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\underline{u}_{t}\geq M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><munder accentunder="true"><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></munder><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>≥</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\underline{u}_{t}\geq M</annotation></semantics></math> when <math id="S3.p13.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\geq\bar{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>≥</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>T</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\geq\bar{T}</annotation></semantics></math>. This implies that <math id="S3.p13.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{t}\geq M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>≥</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{t}\geq M</annotation></semantics></math> when <math id="S3.p13.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\geq\bar{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>≥</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>T</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\geq\bar{T}</annotation></semantics></math>, which violates Assumption <a href="#Thmassumption2" title="Assumption 2. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref ltx_markedasmath ltx_font_italic"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p14" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p14.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p14.1.1" class="ltx_text">Therefore, <math id="S3.p14.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> cannot stay positive in <math id="S3.p14.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(0,\bar{T})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>T</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(0,\bar{T})</annotation></semantics></math>. However, if the deviation ever hits <math id="S3.p14.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> during <math id="S3.p14.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\in(0,\bar{T})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>T</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\in(0,\bar{T})</annotation></semantics></math>, this would also make positive profit for the arbitrageur. Consider the first time the deviation hits <math id="S3.p14.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math>. The payoff in Equation (<a href="#S3.E2" title="In Proof. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) is positive. In sum, if <math id="S3.p14.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{0}&gt;\lambda S_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{0}&gt;\lambda S_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>, the proposed strategy is a random maturity arbitrage.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p15" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p15.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p15.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Scenario 2:<span id="S3.p15.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Next, if <math id="S3.p15.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{0}&lt;\lambda S_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{0}&lt;\lambda S_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e. <math id="S3.p15.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{0}&lt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{0}&lt;0</annotation></semantics></math>, consider the second strategy of longing 1 futures and shorting <math id="S3.p15.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> spot. As before, we want to show that for this strategy under any price path of the perpetual futures and the spot, there always exists a bounded future time <math id="S3.p15.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> such that the strategy payoff is positive, i.e. this is a random maturity arbitrage. Similarly, to prevent the arbitrageur from making a profit, the payoff needs to satisfy:</span></span></p>
<table id="S3.Ex7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e^{-rt}u_{t}\leq u_{0}+(\kappa-r)\int_{0}^{t}u_{s}e^{-rs}ds." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e^{-rt}u_{t}\leq u_{0}+(\kappa-r)\int_{0}^{t}u_{s}e^{-rs}ds.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p15.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p15.2.1" class="ltx_text">Consider the first time period when the deviation is negative, i.e. <math id="S3.p15.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{s}&lt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{s}&lt;0</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.p15.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s\in(0,\min\{t&gt;0,u_{t}=0\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>min</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em">CLOSE</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s\in(0,\min\{t&gt;0,u_{t}=0\}</annotation></semantics></math>. <math id="S3.p15.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e^{-rt}\bar{u}_{t}=u_{0}+(\kappa-r)\int_{0}^{t}\bar{u}_{s}e^{-rs}ds" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>u</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>u</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>s</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e^{-rt}\bar{u}_{t}=u_{0}+(\kappa-r)\int_{0}^{t}\bar{u}_{s}e^{-rs}ds</annotation></semantics></math> provides an upper bound for all processes satisfying the inequality. This is the same integral equation as we see in the first case. We have:</span></p>
<table id="S3.Ex8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{u}_{t}=e^{\kappa t}u_{0}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>u</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{u}_{t}=e^{\kappa t}u_{0}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p15.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p15.3.1" class="ltx_text">From the above expression, there exists <math id="S3.p15.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{T}=\frac{\log(M)-log(-u_{0})}{\kappa}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>T</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{T}=\frac{\log(M)-log(-u_{0})}{\kappa}</annotation></semantics></math> such that <math id="S3.p15.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{u}_{t}&lt;-M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>u</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{u}_{t}&lt;-M</annotation></semantics></math> when <math id="S3.p15.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\geq\bar{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>≥</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>T</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\geq\bar{T}</annotation></semantics></math>. This implies that <math id="S3.p15.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{t}\leq-M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{t}\leq-M</annotation></semantics></math> when <math id="S3.p15.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\geq\bar{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>≥</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>T</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\geq\bar{T}</annotation></semantics></math>, which breaks Assumption <a href="#Thmassumption2" title="Assumption 2. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p16" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p16.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p16.1.1" class="ltx_text">Similar to scenario 1, <math id="S3.p16.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> cannot stay negative in <math id="S3.p16.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(0,\bar{T})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>T</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(0,\bar{T})</annotation></semantics></math>. However, if it ever hits <math id="S3.p16.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> in the period, exiting the position the first time the deviation hits <math id="S3.p16.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> would be a profitable strategy for the arbitrageur. Therefore, if <math id="S3.p16.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{0}&lt;\lambda S_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{0}&lt;\lambda S_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>, the proposed strategy is a random maturity arbitrage.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p17" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p17.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p17.1.1" class="ltx_text">In sum, when there is an absence of random maturity arbitrage strategies, the price of perpetual futures is a fixed constant times the spot price given in Equation (<a href="#S3.E1" title="In Proposition 1 (No-arbitrage price). ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>).</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p18" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p18.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p18.1.1" class="ltx_text">For the opposite direction of proof, when the futures and spot prices satisfy Equation <a href="#S3.E1" title="In Proposition 1 (No-arbitrage price). ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, we need to prove that there is no random maturity arbitrage opportunity in the market. This can be seen easily as any long-short trading strategies would be exposed to the risk in the spot market as long as the proportion is not the same as <math id="S3.p18.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math>. Longing or shorting the spot market is clearly not a random maturity arbitrage opportunity as the time to make a positive arbitrage profit is not bounded for the arbitrageur.
∎</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.p19" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p19.1" class="ltx_p">To gain an intuition for this result, consider the three terms of Equation <a href="#S3.E2" title="In Proof. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. The first term is the spread at unwinding discounted to the present. The second term is the initial spread. The last term is the present value of cumulated funding payments from initiation to unwinding. The last two terms account for gains to the arbitrageur in this scenario. The first term is the source of tension here. For fixed-maturity futures, this spread is guaranteed to be zero at expiration. However, an arbitrageur in perpetual futures faces the risk that when they wish to unwind the trade, the spread may be arbitrarily large.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p20" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p20.1" class="ltx_p">Our key insight is that a positive and even modestly large spread can still leave the arbitrageur with a positive payoff because funding payments also increase with the spread. As long as the spread does not diverge to infinity, there will be some future bounded unwinding time <math id="S3.p20.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> when the accumulated funding rate payments overcome any finite potential losses at unwinding.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p21" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p21.1" class="ltx_p">Note that if we relax the assumption that the short rate is constant for arbitrageurs, this may introduce some additional risk to the four parts of terms in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Proof. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>: (1) mark-to-market changes in futures price; (2) funding-rate payment; (3) reinvestment in the spot market; (4) rollover of the short-term debt. This extension also relates to the literature examining the differences between futures and forwards in the context of stochastic interest rates, such as <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cox et al. (1981)</a></cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grinblatt and Jegadeesh (1996)</a></cite>. They show that marking-to-market introduces an additional term in the futures price related to the covariance between the underlying asset and interest rate. Empirically, however, the volatility in the short rate is considerably smaller than the volatility in the deviation from futures to its fundamental price. Moreover, the changes in the short rate have opposite effects on payment from the cash market and the funding payment, as well as mark-to-market margin in the futures market and reinvestment in the spot market. Therefore, we abstract from short-rate randomness here but note it is an interesting avenue for future work.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p22" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p22.1" class="ltx_p">Empirically, the arbitrageurs face trading costs when opening or terminating their positions. Suppose they face a round-trip trading cost of <math id="S3.p22.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math>. We can derive the no random maturity arbitrage bounds for perpetual futures.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmproposition2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_proposition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmproposition2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proposition 2</span></span><span id="Thmproposition2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(No-arbitrage bound)<span id="Thmproposition2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmproposition2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmproposition2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmproposition2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Under Assumption <a href="#Thmassumption1" title="Assumption 1. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> and <a href="#Thmassumption2" title="Assumption 2. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, when there is a round-trip trading cost <math id="Thmproposition2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> of executing the trading strategy, the absence of random-maturity arbitrage opportunities implies that perpetual futures price will lie within the following bound relative to the spot:</span></p>
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|F_{t}-\frac{\kappa}{\kappa-\left(r-r^{\prime}\right)}S_{t}|\leq C." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><mfrac><mi>κ</mi><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|F_{t}-\frac{\kappa}{\kappa-\left(r-r^{\prime}\right)}S_{t}|\leq C.</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>

</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.3" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="S3.p23" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p23.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p23.1.1" class="ltx_text">Similar to the proof of proposition <a href="#Thmproposition1" title="Proposition 1 (No-arbitrage price). ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, consider the following two scenarios.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p24" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p24.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p24.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Scenario 1<span id="S3.p24.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">: If <math id="S3.p24.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{0}&gt;\lambda S_{0}+C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{0}&gt;\lambda S_{0}+C</annotation></semantics></math>, then we show the strategy of longing <math id="S3.p24.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> spot and shorting <math id="S3.p24.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> futures is a random-maturity arbitrage strategy with trading cost. To prevent the arbitrageur from making a profit, now the payoff needs to satisfy:</span></span></p>
<table id="S3.Ex9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-e^{-rt}u_{t}+u_{0}-C+(\kappa-r)\int_{0}^{t}u_{s}e^{-rs}ds\leq 0." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-e^{-rt}u_{t}+u_{0}-C+(\kappa-r)\int_{0}^{t}u_{s}e^{-rs}ds\leq 0.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p24.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p24.2.1" class="ltx_text">Following the same argument as in the proof of proposition <a href="#Thmproposition1" title="Proposition 1 (No-arbitrage price). ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, we can find the lower bound process <math id="S3.p24.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\underline{u}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><munder accentunder="true"><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></munder><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\underline{u}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> as:</span></p>
<table id="S3.Ex10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\underline{u}_{t}=(u_{0}-C)e^{\kappa t}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><munder accentunder="true"><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></munder><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\underline{u}_{t}=(u_{0}-C)e^{\kappa t}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p24.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p24.3.1" class="ltx_text">When <math id="S3.p24.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{0}&gt;C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{0}&gt;C</annotation></semantics></math>, this process will explode toward <math id="S3.p24.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> at an exponential rate. Following the same argument as in proof proposition <a href="#Thmproposition1" title="Proposition 1 (No-arbitrage price). ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, the proposed trading strategy is a random-maturity arbitrage strategy.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p25" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p25.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p25.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Scenario 2<span id="S3.p25.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">: If <math id="S3.p25.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{0}&lt;\lambda S_{0}-C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{0}&lt;\lambda S_{0}-C</annotation></semantics></math>, then we show the strategy of longing 1 futures and shorting <math id="S3.p25.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> spot is a random-maturity arbitrage strategy despite the trading cost. Now, the payoff needs to satisfy the following condition to prevent the arbitrageur from making a profit:</span></span></p>
<table id="S3.Ex11" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e^{-rt}u_{t}-u_{0}-C-(\kappa-r)\int_{0}^{t}u_{s}e^{-rs}ds\leq 0." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e^{-rt}u_{t}-u_{0}-C-(\kappa-r)\int_{0}^{t}u_{s}e^{-rs}ds\leq 0.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p25.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p25.2.1" class="ltx_text">Similar to the argument in scenario 2 of proposition <a href="#Thmproposition1" title="Proposition 1 (No-arbitrage price). ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, we can find the upper bound process as:</span></p>
<table id="S3.Ex12" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{u}_{t}=(u_{0}+C)e^{\kappa t}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>u</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{u}_{t}=(u_{0}+C)e^{\kappa t}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p25.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p25.3.1" class="ltx_text">When <math id="S3.p25.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{0}&lt;-C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{0}&lt;-C</annotation></semantics></math>, this process will explode toward <math id="S3.p25.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> at an exponential rate. With the same argument, the proposed trading strategy is again a random-maturity arbitrage strategy.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p26" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p26.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p26.1.1" class="ltx_text">In sum, with trading cost, the absence of random maturity arbitrage opportunity implies that the futures price to lie within a bound relative to the spot: <math id="S3.p26.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda S_{t}-C\leq F_{t}\leq\lambda S_{t}+C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda S_{t}-C\leq F_{t}\leq\lambda S_{t}+C</annotation></semantics></math>.
∎</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.p27" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p27.1" class="ltx_p">In the presence of trading costs, when the deviation of perpetual futures price from <math id="S3.p27.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda S_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda S_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, is larger than the round-trip trading costs <math id="S3.p27.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math>, arbitrageurs would have a strong incentive to trade perpetual futures toward the price <math id="S3.p27.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda S_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda S_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>. This proposition also prescribes a trading strategy to exploit the futures-spot divergence in markets with different levels of trading costs. In the next section, we provide an empirical analysis of the futures-spot deviation and present arbitrage trading strategies motivated by our theory.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Data and Empirical Analysis</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We conduct an empirical analysis of perpetual futures arbitrage strategies. We first describe the data. We then measure the deviations of the crypto futures-spot spread from the no-arbitrage benchmark. Finally, we implement a trading strategy that exploits deviations from random-maturity no-arbitrage bounds and quantify the gains from this strategy net of trading costs.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Data</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We focus on the five largest cryptocurrencies excluding stablecoins: Bitcoin (BTC), Ether (ETH), BNB (BNB), Dogecoin (DOGE), and Cardano (ADA) with a total market cap of $1.83 trillion, which account for 73.2% of the total market share of the Crypto market by March 2024.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For each token, we obtain perpetual futures and spot prices at a 1-hour frequency from Binance. Binance is by far the leading exchange in the crypto realm. Another major benefit of using the Binance data is: nearly every part of our trading strategies can be completed within the same platform without delay in transferring funds. As such, it approximates the real-world investment opportunities faced by traders.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We retrieve the perpetual funding rates from Binance. The funding rate is paid every 8 hours on Binance. So we have futures and spot prices every hour and realized funding rate payment at 8:00, 16:00, and 0:00 GMT each day. The perpetual and spot tradings occur 24 hours per day and 7 days a week so there are no after-market hours in this market.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We get the earliest possible data on perpetual futures trading from Binance. The table below lists the starting and ending dates of our data for each cryptocurrency. Our data ends on 2024-03-11, covering the fallout of the FTX.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2: </span>Sample descriptions</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S4.T2.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="S4.T2.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">This table presents the sample start and end dates for the five cryptocurrencies and their total number of observations.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We obtain trading costs from Binance’s website<span id="footnote4" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">4</span>
              
              
              
            <a href="https://www.binance.com/en/fee/trading" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://www.binance.com/en/fee/trading</a> provides data on trading fees in perpetual futures and the spot market</span></span></span>. In general, trading costs for the spot market are significantly larger than those for the perpetual futures for similar trading volume because futures are typically traded with leverage. Fee tiers are attributed to the 30-day trading volume. We attribute high trading costs with a 30-day spot trading volume above $1 million and futures trading volume above $15 million (small individual trader). Medium trading costs are attributed to a 30-day spot trading volume above $150 million and futures trading volume above $1 billion (small funds). Low trading costs are attributed to a 30-day spot trading volume above $2 billion and futures trading volume above 12.5 billion (large funds). Zero fees can be negotiated with customized contracts, for example, for market makers. We consider trading costs for makers instead of takers because institutions typically trade maker orders.<span id="footnote5" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">5</span>
              
              
              
            Takers trade market orders while makers trade limit orders. Takers take liquidity from the market while makers make the market or provide liquidity to the market.</span></span></span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.1 Data ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> presents the specification of different trading costs. It also shows the random-maturity arbitrage bound for the deviation between the perpetual futures and the no-arbitrage price (<math id="S4.SS1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS1.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{u}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{u}</annotation></semantics></math>). The bounds become wider as the trading costs increase. Detailed explanations of the trading costs specifications are also provided in appendix Figure <a href="#Sx1.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ A. Additional Figures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> and Figure <a href="#Sx1.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ A. Additional Figures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>.</p>
</div>

<td id="S4.T3.2.4.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right">-114.4%</td>
<td id="S4.T3.2.4.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right">114.3%</td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T3.2.5" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S4.T3.2.5.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_bb">High</th>
<td id="S4.T3.2.5.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb">0.0675%</td>
<td id="S4.T3.2.5.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb">0.0144%</td>
<td id="S4.T3.2.5.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb">-179.5%</td>
<td id="S4.T3.2.5.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb">179.2%</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 3: </span>Trading costs tiers</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S4.T3.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="S4.T3.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Fee tiers are assigned based on past 30-day trading volume. High fees correspond to a 30-day trading volume above $1mn in spot and above $15mn in perpetuals, typically an individual trader. Medium fees attribute to a 30-day trading volume above $150mn in spot and above $1bn in perpetuals (small funds). Low fees are attributed to a 30-day trading volume above $2bn in spot and above $12.5bn in perpetuals (large funds). The no-fee tier can be negotiated with customized contracts, for example for market makers. We also report the theory implied no arbitrage bound (<math id="S4.T3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.T3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{u}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{u}</annotation></semantics></math>) for <math id="S4.T3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> under different trading costs specifications. They are calculated using the following formulas: <math id="S4.T3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{l}=\kappa log\left(1-C\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{l}=\kappa log\left(1-C\right)</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.T3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{u}=\kappa log\left(1+C\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{u}=\kappa log\left(1+C\right)</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S4.T3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> is the round-trip percentage trading costs of the long-short strategy of perpetual and spot.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">In addition to the direct trading fees, traders also face bid-ask spread and price impact costs in our arbitrage strategies. To assess the importance of such indirect trading costs, we attain from Kaiko a high-frequency sample with one month of order book snapshots taken every 30 seconds. With this data, we estimate that the average bid-ask spread for perpetual futures is less than 0.05 bps, and the price impact of a trade with a size equal to 0.5 million is less than 0.3 bps. Combined, these indirect costs are less than 0.35 bps, which is substantially smaller than our direct trading fees. Therefore, we focus our analysis on the direct trading fees, as they are the dominant form of trading costs for our arbitrage strategies.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">To measure the deviation from the no-arbitrage price, we also obtain the interest rate data from Aave, a leading open-source DeFi liquidity protocol. Customers on Aave can either be a supplier or a borrower of cryptocurrencies. Because of the anonymity and decentralization of DeFi system, all borrowings are over-collateralized and the collateral can serve as an additional supply to the system for borrowing. The customers can also supply spare currencies to the system to earn an interest rate. The supply interest rate is typically different from the borrowing interest rate. Both interest rates and their wedge are determined algorithmically based on the market condition of supply and demand. We use interest rates from this platform because we believe it is a good proxy for the funding condition in the crypto market. Our results are robust if we use the interest rate from the traditional financial market.<span id="footnote6" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">6</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">6</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">6</span>
              
              
              
            We also run our analysis using daily T-bill rates obtained from Kenneth French’s website at <a href="https://mba.tuck.dartmouth.edu/pages/faculty/ken.french/Data_Library/f-f_factors.html" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://mba.tuck.dartmouth.edu/pages/faculty/ken.french/Data_Library/f-f_factors.html</a>. The results are very close to ones using crypto market supply and borrowing rates.</span></span></span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p9.1" class="ltx_p">Our theory indicates using a risk-free rate available to the arbitrageurs. Therefore, we consider the interest rates on the stablecoins, which are not subject to volatile spot price movement and are the currency of denomination for perpetual futures margins. There are three major stablecoins traded on Aave: USDT, USDC, and DAI. To get a robust measure of the risk-free rate, we take an average of the three interest rates to arrive at our final risk-free supply and borrowing rate for the arbitrageurs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p10.1" class="ltx_p">We plot the time-series evolvement of the interest rate in the appendix Figure <a href="#Sx1.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ A. Additional Figures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>. During the early years, we see higher interest rate volatility due to the funding liquidity of the DeFi platform. In later samples, interest rates are more stable and approach interest rates in traditional financial markets.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p11.1" class="ltx_p">Our interest rate data starts from 2020-01-08. Therefore, for coins with perpetual data available before the time (BTC and ETH), we begin the analysis from 2020-01-08. For other coins (BNB, DOGE, ADA), we begin the analysis from the time when they have data available.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Deviations of perpetual futures from no-arbitrage benchmarks</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The focus of our empirical analysis is the annualized deviation <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>, defined as the interest rate spread that would rationalize an observed future-spot spread:</p>
<table id="S4.Ex13" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex13.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F=S\,\frac{\kappa}{\kappa-(r+\rho-r^{\prime})}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><mi>κ</mi><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>ρ</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F=S\,\frac{\kappa}{\kappa-(r+\rho-r^{\prime})}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">For example, an estimated <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> of 1 percent would mean that borrowing costs in the cash market faced by arbitrageurs would have to be one percentage point higher than the prevailing interest rate <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> in the cash market for the futures-spot gap to be arbitrage-free.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Using <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> to denote <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="log(F)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">log(F)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="log(S)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">log(S)</annotation></semantics></math> respectively, we obtain the following approximate equation for <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S4.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=\kappa\left(1-e^{-(f-s)}\right)-(r-r^{\prime})\approx\kappa(f-s)-(r-r^{\prime})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=\kappa\left(1-e^{-(f-s)}\right)-(r-r^{\prime})\approx\kappa(f-s)-(r-r^{\prime}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">This definition is the same in spirit to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du et al. (2018)</a></cite>, who measure covered interest parity (CIP) deviations with the wedge that would equate the dollar borrowing rate and the synthetic dollar borrowing rate. For the rest of our paper, we focus on the approximate measure and note that, in our setting, no interest is paid on spot crypto holdings (<math id="S4.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r^{\prime}=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>r</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r^{\prime}=0</annotation></semantics></math>).<span id="footnote7" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">7</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">7</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">7</span>
              
              
              
            The difference between the exact and the approximate measure is negligible.</span></span></span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Each hour, we calculate <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> defined in Equation (<a href="#S4.E5" title="In 4.2 Deviations of perpetual futures from no-arbitrage benchmarks ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>) using data on the perpetual futures price, spot price, and the crypto risk-free interest rate. When the perpetual futures price is above the spot, an arbitrageur would short the futures and long the spot, and would finance her position by borrowing in the cash market (as is shown in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Proof. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>). Therefore, we use the borrowing rate from Aave as the risk-free rate. On the other hand, when the perpetual futures price is below the spot, an arbitrageur would long the futures, short the spot, and invest the proceeds from shorting in the cash market (as is shown in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Proof. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>). In such cases, we use the supply rate from Aave as the risk-free rate.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<div id="S4.F3.2" class="ltx_logical-block ltx_figure_panel">

</div>
        
</div></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>Deviations of perpetual futures from no-arbitrage benchmarks</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
