</tbody>
</table></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 4: </span>Summary Statistics for Deviations from No-arbitrage Prices</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S4.T4.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="S4.T4.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">The table below summarizes statistics for <math id="S4.T4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.T4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\rho|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\rho|</annotation></semantics></math> across various crypto tokens. <math id="S4.T4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{NW}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>W</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{NW}</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to the Newey-West adjusted p-value, testing the null hypothesis that the mean <math id="S4.T4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> (or <math id="S4.T4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\rho|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\rho|</annotation></semantics></math>) is zero. The sample periods are shown in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.1 Data ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 4.2 Deviations of perpetual futures from no-arbitrage benchmarks ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> reports summary statistics for <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\rho|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\rho|</annotation></semantics></math> in our sample. As can be seen, the mean future-spot spread is modest, lying between <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-2</annotation></semantics></math> and 12 percentage points. The p-values show we cannot reject the hypothesis that the deviations are zero on average. Thus, on average our theoretical prices provide a useful benchmark.
Around this benchmark, however, perpetual futures prices vary significantly from spot prices. The mean absolute deviation is about 60% to 90% per year across different cryptocurrency tokens. Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 Deviations of perpetual futures from no-arbitrage benchmarks ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> depicts the 7-day moving average of <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> for each of the five examined cryptocurrencies. It reveals considerable comovement in futures-spot spreads across these cryptocurrencies, suggesting a common factor at play that drives the observed divergence. This observation is corroborated by Table <span class="ltx_ref ltx_missing_label ltx_ref_self"></span>, which demonstrates high correlations among futures-spot deviations across the different cryptocurrencies. This trend underscores the interconnectedness of cryptocurrency markets and is consistent with the comovement of traditional currencies documented by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lustig, Roussanov, and Verdelhan (2011)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">One hypothesis for this significant comovement in <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> across various cryptocurrencies pertains to time-varying funding constraints encountered by arbitrageurs in the market <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brunnermeier and Pedersen, 2009</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Garleanu and Pedersen, 2011</a>)</cite>. Because arbitrageurs often serve as marginal traders in all markets, their funding constraints are potentially reflected in the <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> across all major cryptocurrency markets. Our theoretical and empirical analyses underscore the importance of measuring <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>. Doing so not only sheds light on potential market stress but also provides a gauge for the shadow costs associated with the trading and funding constraints arbitrageurs face.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Conversely, from the demand side, shared sentiment across various cryptocurrencies could also contribute to explaining the concurrent movement of <math id="S4.SS2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> across different markets. Our theoretical analysis suggests that arbitrageurs will only meet the market demand if the price deviation surpasses the combined trading and funding costs. As a result, the overall market sentiment in the futures market relative to the spot market becomes evident in the price difference between futures and spot prices. If the sentiment across different markets is influenced by a common factor, we would anticipate a significant comovement in the futures-spot spread. In Section <a href="#S5" title="5 Explaining Futures-spot Deviations ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, we delve deeper into explaining the futures-spot spread. Our results demonstrate that the past returns of each cryptocurrency serve as significant explanatory variables for the time-series variation in the spread.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Interestingly, the correlation between deviations and spot market returns is quite modest. Although spot market returns are highly correlated among themselves, in line with the strong market factor results from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2022)</a></cite>, and no-arbitrage price deviations are highly correlated among themselves, it appears that different forces drive these distinct phenomena.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Furthermore, we find that after the year 2022, futures-spot spreads become smaller in magnitude and less volatile compared to earlier years. The 7-day moving average stays around -50% most of the time for the five cryptocurrencies while larger sways in earlier years are quite common. This suggests the market is becoming increasingly efficient. In terms of the sign of the deviation, which appears to stabilize at the negative region, two forces are potentially at play: (1) on the futures customer end, the relative demand in the futures market is weaker compared to the spot; (2) for arbitrageurs, because of the lack of infrastructure to short the cryptos in the spot market (high shorting costs), their funding constraints would be larger in the negative region. All these forces contribute to the stabilization of the futures spot deviation around <math id="S4.SS2.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-50</annotation></semantics></math> percentage points.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p9.1" class="ltx_p">Last but not least, by design, <math id="S4.SS2.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> is also highly correlated with the funding rate. The funding rate does not correlate perfectly with <math id="S4.SS2.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> because in real-world implementations: (1) there is a clamp region, within which the funding rate is fixed at 0.01%; (2) the funding rate is calculated as a weighted average of futures-spot price deviations, with larger weight given to more recent observations; (3) in calculating the funding rate, Binance does not just consider the quote price, they also use an impact margin notional to consider price impact of the trade.<span id="footnote8" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">8</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">8</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">8</span>
              
              
              
            See <a href="https://www.binance.com/en/support/faq/360033525031" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://www.binance.com/en/support/faq/360033525031</a> for details of the funding rate calculation.</span></span></span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We next provide a trading strategy motivated by our random-maturity arbitrage theory. Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.1 Data ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> reports for different trading cost tiers, the bounds (<math id="S4.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{u}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{u}</annotation></semantics></math>) beyond which there exist random-maturity arbitrage opportunities. We consider a simple trading strategy: whenever <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> enters the region outside the annualized round-trip trading costs in Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.1 Data ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, we open the position. We close the position when <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> first goes back to 0.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2212.06888v5/figure_trading_theory_naive_BTC.png" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/243;" width="476" height="243" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy: Bitcoin, high trading costs</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S4.F4.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="S4.F4.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Futures-spot deviations and trading thresholds of the random-maturity arbitrage strategy we implement for BTC under high trading costs. Each blue dot in the figure represents the hourly deviation of futures from the spot <math id="S4.F4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=\kappa(f-s)-r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=\kappa(f-s)-r</annotation></semantics></math>. The number is annualized for ease of interpretation. The orange line is the open-position threshold, and the red line is the close-position threshold.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.3 Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> provides an illustration of the trading strategy. When the deviation is beyond the orange lines, the strategy opens a trading position. The position is closed when the futures/spot deviation first hits the red line. We present trading thresholds across different trading costs for different currencies in Figure <a href="#Sx1.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ A. Additional Figures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> in the appendix. Different trading strategies have the same close-position line which is equal to <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> while the open-position line adjusts to the level of trading costs. In Appendix C, we also present the performance of a data-driven strategy that determines the open and close threshold optimally using the past 6-month data. The data-driven strategy can potentially improve upon this simpler strategy.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Since our trading strategy is a threshold trading rule, to annualize Sharpe ratios we follow <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lucca and Moench (2015)</a></cite>, which considers a trading strategy that is only active on FOMC announcement dates. We first calculate the mean (<math id="S4.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>μ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu</annotation></semantics></math>) and standard deviation (<math id="S4.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math>) of our trading strategy during the time it is active. Next, we scale <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu/\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>σ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu/\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> by the number of periods the strategy is active in a year:</p>
<table id="S4.Ex14" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex14.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="SR=\frac{\mu}{\sigma}\sqrt{N_{a}}\ ," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mi>μ</mi><mi>σ</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></msqrt></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.500em">,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">SR=\frac{\mu}{\sigma}\sqrt{N_{a}}\ ,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>μ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> are average hourly returns and <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{a}</annotation></semantics></math> is the average number of hours the strategy is active in a year. We follow the same approach to annualize the returns and standard deviations: <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{ann}=\mu N_{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{ann}=\mu N_{a}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{ann}=\sigma\sqrt{N_{a}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></msqrt></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{ann}=\sigma\sqrt{N_{a}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T5" class="ltx_table">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure ltx_flex_table">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<table id="S4.T5.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<thead class="ltx_thead">
<tr id="S4.T5.2.1" class="ltx_tr">

<tr id="S4.T5.2.2" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S4.T5.2.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_th ltx_th_row"></th>
<th id="S4.T5.2.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_th_row"></th>
<th id="S4.T5.2.2.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_t"><span id="S4.T5.2.2.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">No</span></th>
<th id="S4.T5.2.2.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_t"><span id="S4.T5.2.2.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">Low</span></th>
<th id="S4.T5.2.2.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_t"><span id="S4.T5.2.2.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">Medium</span></th>
<th id="S4.T5.2.2.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_t"><span id="S4.T5.2.2.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">High</span></th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="S4.T5.2.3" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S4.T5.2.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_t"><span id="S4.T5.2.3.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">BTC</span></th>
<th id="S4.T5.2.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_t"><span id="S4.T5.2.3.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">SR</span></th>
<td id="S4.T5.2.3.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_t"><span id="S4.T5.2.3.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">3.53</span></td>

</table></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 5: </span>Performance of Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S4.T5.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="S4.T5.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Performance under different trading cost tiers. The fees for spot (futures) are 2.25 (0.18) bps, 4.5 (0.72) bps, and 6.75 (1.44) bps for the low, medium, and high trading cost levels. Statistics reported are the annualized Sharpe ratio, return (%), volatility (%), max drawdown (%), alpha (%), t-stat of the alpha, proportion of time the strategy is active (%), and average open-to-close (OtC) position duration in hours. The returns reported are excess returns from the random maturity arbitrage strategies. The 3-factor data from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2022)</a></cite> used to calculate alpha ends on April 9th 2023.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 4.3 Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> presents the strategy’s performance under different fee tiers. As trading costs decrease, the random-maturity arbitrage strategy engages in more active trading, leading to an increase in the SRs and a decrease in the average duration of open-to-close positions. The strategy also delivers highly significant alphas relative to the 3-factor model by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2022)</a></cite> and the 5-factor model by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cong et al. (2022a)</a></cite>. Evidently, the strategy’s performance cannot be explained by previously suggested risk factors.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ 4.3 Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> and Table <a href="#S4.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ 4.3 Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> zoom in and present the trading performance of the strategy under high trading costs. We consider two cases: (1) unrestricted and (2) long-spot only. We consider the second case because, in earlier years of crypto derivatives, the infrastructure for shorting cryptocurrencies was not well-developed. We find that, as is implied by our theory, whenever the deviation between futures and spot is larger than the trading costs, performing a random-maturity arbitrage strategy would generate returns with high SR. After trading costs, the strategy generates an SR of 1.80 for BTC and much higher SRs for other cryptocurrencies.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 6: </span>Performance of Unrestricted Trading Strategy Over Time: High Trading Costs Tier</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S4.T6.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="S4.T6.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">This table presents the Sharpe ratios, annualized returns (%), standard deviations (%), maximum drawdowns (%), active percentages (%), and the average open-to-close time (hours) of the unrestricted random-maturity arbitrage trading strategies for five different cryptocurrencies with high trading costs. For the unrestricted trading strategy, both longing and shorting the spot are allowed. The returns reported are excess returns from the random maturity arbitrage strategies.</span></p></div></div>

</table></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 7: </span>Performance of Long-spot-only Trading Strategy Over Time: High Trading Costs Tier</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S4.T7.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="S4.T7.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">This table presents the Sharpe ratios, annualized returns (%), standard deviations (%), maximum drawdowns (%), active percentages (%), and the average open-to-close time (hours) of the long-spot only random-maturity arbitrage trading strategies for five different cryptocurrencies with high trading costs. For the long-spot only strategy, shorting the spot is not allowed. The returns reported are excess returns from the random maturity arbitrage strategies. In 2022, for ADA, there is no positive deviation of <math id="S4.T7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">rho</annotation></semantics></math> from the high-trading cost threshold. Therefore, the trading strategy is not active during the year for ADA.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ 4.3 Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> also shows that over time, the perpetual futures market seems to become more efficient. As we can see in 2022, the deviation of crypto price from the arbitrage-free bound is less frequent compared to earlier years. But when the deviation happens, the resulting SR from the trade remains high.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Comparing the results with <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du, Tepper, and Verdelhan (2018)</a></cite>, we find that deviations in crypto perpetual futures are considerably larger in magnitude. As a result, gains from the arbitrage strategies we study are also larger. Even though the volatility of the trading strategy also scales up, the Sharpe ratios in the crypto space are still larger than those in the traditional foreign exchange market, as reported in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du, Tepper, and Verdelhan (2018)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p8.1" class="ltx_p">When a futures-spot gap opens up, gains from the trading strategy could potentially arise from two main sources: price convergence and funding rate payments. While industry publications usually emphasize the funding rate channel, we note that price convergence can generate quicker gains from arbitrage if dislocations are short-lived.
To examine these two sources empirically, in Table <a href="#S4.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ 4.3 Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>, we provide a decomposition of the trading strategy’s performance into price convergence versus funding rate payment. We find that price convergence plays a dominant role in total trading returns, while funding rate payments have a more minor role, which seems to diminish over time.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 8: </span>Return Decomposition: Price Convergence vs Funding Rate Payment for Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategies</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S4.T8.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="S4.T8.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">This table decomposes the portfolio return into the part due to price convergence and the part due to funding rate payment. The returns reported are excess returns from the random-maturity arbitrage strategies. There are a few negative funding rate payments due to the difference in the empirical specification of funding rate payment (see Appendix B for detail) with our theoretical framework when the deviation is small.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p9.1" class="ltx_p">The success of the trading strategy supports the theory of random-maturity arbitrage. Whenever there is a deviation larger than the gap implied by the theory, betting on convergence tends to generate a positive payoff at some uncertain future time. Therefore, the convergence arbitrage trade generates high Sharpe ratios.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Explaining Futures-spot Deviations</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">From Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 Deviations of perpetual futures from no-arbitrage benchmarks ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, we observe a strong common comovement of the futures-spot deviation across all crypto assets. Our goal is to understand the fundamental forces driving this common factor. We consider two potential hypotheses: (1) the time-varying funding constraints of arbitrageurs and (2) the time-varying relative demand from end-users for perpetual futures compared to the spot.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Both forces could potentially explain these patterns. Arbitrageurs will accommodate the relative demand from end-users only until the price deviation lies within the random-maturity no-arbitrage bound, which depends on arbitrageurs’ funding conditions. As arbitrageurs are likely the marginal investors in all cryptocurrency markets, their time-varying funding constraints may create common time-series variation in <math id="S5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> across different cryptocurrencies.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">On the other hand, when the deviation lies within the no-arbitrage bound, variations in demand from the perpetual futures market compared to the spot market will influence the price deviation. It is plausible that relative demand has common factors across different cryptocurrencies. For instance, sentiment could drive their common variation, as perpetual futures allow for high leverage, which attracts overconfident, extrapolative, and sentiment-driven investors.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Determining which of the two factors better explains the observed price deviation is an empirical question. To shed light on this, we use past returns as a proxy for relative extrapolative demand in the perpetual futures market compared to the spot market. Past returns correlate with the demand from investors with extrapolative beliefs, who are more likely to trade in the perpetual futures market, given the high leverage it provides. Therefore, past returns would correlate with the relative demand in the perpetual futures market compared to the spot.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p5.1" class="ltx_p">For the time-varying funding constraint, we consider using crypto return volatility as a proxy because, as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Adrian and Shin (2010)</a></cite>, arbitrageurs likely face Value-at-Risk (VaR) type constraints, which are more likely to bind when market volatility is high.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Moreover, from Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 Deviations of perpetual futures from no-arbitrage benchmarks ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, we see a downward trend for the magnitude of the deviation. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kondor (2009)</a></cite>’s model of convergence trading predicts that greater competition amoung arbitrageurs reduces the profitability of arbitrage opportunities and deviations approach a martingale. Therefore, we add a time trend variable to the regression to test if the market becomes more efficient as more arbitrageurs and capital competes in this market.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p7.1" class="ltx_p">In sum, the regression models can be represented as:</p>
<table id="S5.EGx4" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S5.E6"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S5.E6.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle\rho_{i,t}=\beta_{0,i}+\beta_{1}(t/365)+\beta_{2}R_{i,t-120:t-1}+\beta_{3}\sigma_{i,t-120:t-1}+\epsilon_{i,t}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>β</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>365</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>120</mn></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><msub><mi>σ</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>120</mn></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\rho_{i,t}=\beta_{0,i}+\beta_{1}(t/365)+\beta_{2}R_{i,t-120:t-1}+\beta_{3}\sigma_{i,t-120:t-1}+\epsilon_{i,t},</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<tbody id="S5.E7"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S5.E7.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle|\rho_{i,t}|=\beta_{0,i}+\beta_{1}(t/365)+\beta_{2}R_{i,t-120:t-1}+\beta_{3}\sigma_{i,t-120:t-1}+\epsilon_{i,t}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">|</mo><mo lspace="0.167em">=</mo><msub><mi>β</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>365</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>120</mn></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><msub><mi>σ</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>120</mn></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle|\rho_{i,t}|=\beta_{0,i}+\beta_{1}(t/365)+\beta_{2}R_{i,t-120:t-1}+\beta_{3}\sigma_{i,t-120:t-1}+\epsilon_{i,t},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.p7.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S5.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{i,t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{i,t}</annotation></semantics></math> represents the futures-spot deviation, <math id="S5.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{0,i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>β</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{0,i}</annotation></semantics></math> is the currency fixed effect, <math id="S5.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of days since the beginning of the sample, <math id="S5.p7.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="R_{i,t-120:t-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>R</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>120</mn></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{i,t-120:t-1}</annotation></semantics></math> is the annualized spot return to currency <math id="S5.p7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> over the past 120 days, and <math id="S5.p7.m6" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\sigma_{i,t-120:t-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>120</mn></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{i,t-120:t-1}</annotation></semantics></math> is the annualized standard deviation of spot return of currency <math id="S5.p7.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> over the past 120 days. Since we scale the time trend by the number of trading days in a year, the regression coefficient <math id="S5.p7.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> has an interpretation of the average annual change in the futures-spot deviation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S5.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ 5 Explaining Futures-spot Deviations ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> presents the regression results. The regression coefficients on the time trend are negative and highly significant for both <math id="S5.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\rho|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\rho|</annotation></semantics></math>, indicating that the futures-spot gap has been decreasing both in level and in magnitude over time on average. Throughout our sample, on average, <math id="S5.p8.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\rho|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\rho|</annotation></semantics></math> shrinks about 11% per year, which accumulates to over 44% over the whole sample. This indicates that the perpetual futures market is becoming more efficient over time.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T9" class="ltx_table">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure ltx_flex_table">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 9: </span>Regression of the futures-spot gap against explanatory variables</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S5.T9.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="S5.T9.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">We present regression results of <math id="S5.T9.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.T9.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\rho|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\rho|</annotation></semantics></math> on a time trend (Time) measured in units of years, past 120 days’ annualized returns (Ret), and volatility (Vol) in the spot market. We add a currency fixed effect to the regression and consider three specifications: (1) regressing <math id="S5.T9.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>/<math id="S5.T9.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\rho|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\rho|</annotation></semantics></math> on the time trend, (2) regressing <math id="S5.T9.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>/<math id="S5.T9.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\rho|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\rho|</annotation></semantics></math> on past returns, and (3) regressing <math id="S5.T9.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>/<math id="S5.T9.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\rho|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\rho|</annotation></semantics></math> on past returns and volatility. The observations are at a daily frequency. The sample period spans from January 8, 2020 to March 11, 2024, totaling 1,495 days. The table also reports the <math id="S5.T9.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> values for each regression model. We report Newey-West t-statistics in parentheses with a lag of 120 days. <math id="S5.T9.m14" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="*\text{ }p&lt;.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><mtext> </mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>.1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">*\text{ }p&lt;.1</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.T9.m15" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="**\text{ }p&lt;.05" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0em">∗</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><mtext> </mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>.05</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">**\text{ }p&lt;.05</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.T9.m16" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="***\text{ }p&lt;.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0em">∗</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∗</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><mtext> </mtext><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>.01</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">***\text{ }p&lt;.01</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S5.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p9.1" class="ltx_p">The coefficients on past returns are positive and highly significant for both <math id="S5.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\rho|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\rho|</annotation></semantics></math>. This suggests that when past returns are high, perpetual futures exhibit a more positive deviation against the spot. Mapping this back to our second hypothesis, when past returns are high, the demand for futures relative to the spot is also likely to be high. Consequently, even after arbitrageurs accommodate the demand outside of trading costs, the residual demand still manifests itself through the perpetual-spot deviation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p10.1" class="ltx_p">This observation on limits to arbitrage is related to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Makarov and Schoar (2020)</a></cite> which finds that crypto price deviations across international exchanges tend to comove with one another. The driving force behind this comovement is investors’ buying pressure across various countries, with cross-country capital controls serving as the primary impediment to arbitrage capital. In the context of perpetual futures, end-user demand contributes to the comovement of different cryptocurrencies. The limits to arbitrage predominantly manifest in the form of trading frictions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p11.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu and Tsyvinski (2021)</a></cite> document a significant time-series momentum pattern in the crypto market. Given that positive past returns lead to a positive gap between futures and spot prices, it is worth examining further whether the time-series momentum phenomenon is driven by margin trading and price pressure from the perpetual futures market. We leave this as an open question for future research.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p12" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p12.1" class="ltx_p">We find that volatility does not significantly covary with <math id="S5.p12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\rho|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\rho|</annotation></semantics></math>. This suggests that time-varying funding constraints of arbitrageurs do not drive the comovement in futures-spot deviations across different cryptocurrencies.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p13" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p13.1" class="ltx_p">In summary, a prerequisite for the gap between futures and spot prices to occur is the existence of trading costs for arbitrageurs. Arbitrage trading will accommodate all the demand in the futures until the price deviation is within a trading cost bound. Within the bound, the relative demand of futures compared to the spot will still manifest itself in the deviation of futures prices from the spot. Due to the comovement of the time-varying relative demand, we observe a significant common factor in crypto future-spot deviations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Perpetual futures play an important role in today’s crypto markets and could potentially be adopted in non-crypto markets in the future. Understanding the fundamental mechanism of this financial derivative is a crucial first step for understanding speculation and hedging dynamics in this fast-evolving area. We provide a comprehensive analysis of the arbitrage and funding rate payment mechanisms that underpin perpetual futures.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In an ideal, frictionless world, we show that arbitrageurs would trade perpetual futures in such a way that a constant proportional relationship would hold between the futures price and the spot price. In the presence of trading costs, the deviation of the futures price from the spot would lie within a bound.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Our derivation focuses on the most salient features of perpetual futures as they are traded on modern crypto markets and abstracts from others. Subsequent work by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ackerer et al. (2023)</a></cite> generalizes our results to various perpetual contracts in both discrete and continuous-time. By relying on the more standard martingale approach to no-arbitrage pricing, their work can incorporate several realistic features of these markets. It can be shown, however, that the transversality assumption central to their analysis implies that strategies aimed at arbitrage of deviations from their benchmark prices are necessarily random-maturity arbitrage strategies, as we argue here. Another interesting avenue for future work is to quantify the practical importance of incorporating these and other real-world details.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Motivated by our theory, we empirically examine the comovement of the futures-spot spread across different cryptocurrencies and implement a theory-motivated arbitrage strategy. We find that this simple strategy yields substantial Sharpe ratios across various trading cost scenarios. The evidence supports our theoretical argument that perpetual futures-spot spreads exceeding trading costs represent a random-maturity arbitrage opportunity.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, we provide an explanation for the common comovement in futures-spot spreads across different crypto-currencies: arbitrageurs can only accommodate market demand if the price deviation exceeds trading costs. As a result, the overall sentiment in the futures market relative to the spot market is reflected in the spread.
Our empirical findings suggest that past return momentum can account for a significant portion of the time-series variation in the futures-spot spread.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>

<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="Sx1.F5.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="Sx1.F5.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">This figure presents the perpetual futures trading view on Binance. The key information includes the futures price (Mark), spot price (Index), real-time funding rate based on the rolling average of the past 8 hours’ observations, and countdown toward funding rate payment (Funding / Countdown) (illustrated with a red rectangle). In this example, futures are trading at a lower price than the spot. The funding rate is negative and is to be paid in 1 hour and 12 minutes.</span></p></div></div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span>Trading costs tiers for the spot market</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="Sx1.F6.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="Sx1.F6.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">This figure presents the trading cost tiers for the crypto spot market from Binance: <a href="https://www.binance.com/en/fee/trading" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://www.binance.com/en/fee/trading</a>. Our high, medium, and low trading cost specification corresponds to VIP 1, VIP 5, and VIP 8 tiers, as illustrated with red rectangles in the picture. The 30-day trading volume requirements for VIP 1, 5, and 8 are 1 million, 150 million, and 2 billion, respectively, in the spot market. We consider the trading costs for makers as institutions typically trade maker orders. Binance offers a temporary discount for VIP 4-8 to have the same trading cost as VIP 9. We consider the non-discounted trading costs to make the comparison more reliable and fair.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 7: </span>Trading costs tiers for the perp market</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="Sx1.F7.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="Sx1.F7.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">This figure presents the trading cost tiers for the crypto perpetual market from Binance: <a href="https://www.binance.com/en/fee/trading" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://www.binance.com/en/fee/trading</a>. Our high, medium, and low trading cost specification corresponds to VIP 1, VIP 5, and VIP 8 tiers, as illustrated with red rectangles in the picture. The 30-day trading volume requirements for VIP 1, 5, and 8 are 15 million, 1 billion, and 12.5 billion, respectively, in the perpetual market. We consider the trading costs for makers as institutions typically trade maker orders.</span></p></div></div>

<figure id="Sx1.F8" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2212.06888v5/interest_rate.svg" id="Sx1.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/238;" width="476" height="238"></object></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 8: </span>Annualized interest rate from Aave</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="Sx1.F8.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="Sx1.F8.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">This figure presents the daily supply and borrowing rate from Aave. We consider three stablecoins: USDT, USDC, and DAI. Each day, we take the average interest rate of the three crypto stablecoins to get the proxy for the risk-free funding rate of the arbitrageurs. The averaging removes the idiosyncratic noise in borrowing and supply in individual stablecoins. The sample period is from 2020-01-08 to 2024-03-11.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
