<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 9: </span>Trading Strategy Visualization: Random-maturity Arbitrage</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="Sx1.F9.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="Sx1.F9.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">This figure presents the random-maturity arbitrage strategy motivated by the theory. The orange, green, and purple lines correspond to the open-position threshold under high, medium, and low trading costs. The red line represents the close-position threshold.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
<section id="Sx2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">B. Funding Rate Calculation on Binance</h2>

<div id="Sx2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we discuss in more detail the funding rate mechanism on the Binance platform based on the methodology given on the Binance website.<span id="footnote9" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">9</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">9</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">9</span>
            
            
            
          <a href="https://www.binance.com/en/support/faq/360033525031" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://www.binance.com/en/support/faq/360033525031</a></span></span></span></p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">There are five general steps in obtaining the funding rate. The first step is to find the Impact Bid/Ask Price Series in a given funding period by analyzing the order book and determining the average fill price to execute a certain notional value (Impact Margin Notional) on the bid and ask sides.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The impact margin notional is defined as the notional available to trade with a margin of 200 USD. So it can be calculated using the following equation:</p>
<table id="Sx2.Ex15" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="Sx2.Ex15.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{IMN}=200/\text{Initial margin rate at maximum leverage level}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>IMN</mtext><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>200</mn><mo>/</mo><mtext>Initial margin rate at maximum leverage level</mtext></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{IMN}=200/\text{Initial margin rate at maximum leverage level}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Given the definition of impact margin notional, the impact bid/ask price is defined as the average trade price after a market sell/buy order with the total quoted notional quantity given by the IMN.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Given impact bid and ask prices (denoted as IBP and IAP, respectively), the second step is to calculate the premium index (denoted as P) series every <math id="Sx2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5</annotation></semantics></math> seconds using the following equation:</p>
<table id="Sx2.Ex16" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="Sx2.Ex16.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P=[\text{Max}(0,\text{IBP}-\text{Price Index})-\text{Max}(0,\text{Price Index}-\text{IAP})]/\text{Price Index}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mtext>Max</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><mtext>IBP</mtext><mo>−</mo><mtext>Price Index</mtext></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mtext>Max</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><mtext>Price Index</mtext><mo>−</mo><mtext>IAP</mtext></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mtext>Price Index</mtext></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P=[\text{Max}(0,\text{IBP}-\text{Price Index})-\text{Max}(0,\text{Price Index}-\text{IAP})]/\text{Price Index},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="Sx2.p5.2" class="ltx_p">where ‘Price Index’ is the weighted average spot price of the underlying asset listed on major spot exchanges.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">The rationale behind this formula is to capture the relative difference between the perpetual contract’s price and the underlying asset’s price, taking into account the actual market liquidity and depth represented by the IBP and IAP.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">The third step is to calculate the time-weighted average premium index over the funding period (8 hours for Binance) using the premium index series:</p>
<table id="Sx2.Ex17" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="Sx2.Ex17.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{P}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_{t}P_{t}/\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_{t}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></munderover><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em">/</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></munderover><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{P}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_{t}P_{t}/\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_{t},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="Sx2.p7.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="Sx2.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the <math id="Sx2.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>-th 5-second in the 8-hour funding period, <math id="Sx2.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{t}=t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{t}=t</annotation></semantics></math> is the weight for each observation, and <math id="Sx2.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> is the total number of 5-second intervals within the 8-hour period. For Binance, <math id="Sx2.p7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=12\times 6\times 8=5760" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>12</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>6</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>5760</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=12\times 6\times 8=5760</annotation></semantics></math>. With this weighting scheme, the observations closer to the funding rate payment receive larger weights. The weights decrease linearly in time over the 8-hour interval.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Given the average premium index, the fourth step is to calculate the funding rate using the equation below:</p>
<table id="Sx2.Ex18" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="Sx2.Ex18.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="fr=\bar{P}+\text{clamp}(\gamma-\bar{P},-0.05\%,0.05\%)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mrow><mtext>clamp</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo>−</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>0.05</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>0.05</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">fr=\bar{P}+\text{clamp}(\gamma-\bar{P},-0.05\%,0.05\%),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="Sx2.p8.2" class="ltx_p">where fr is the funding rate, <math id="Sx2.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> is the interest component set by Binance, and</p>
<table id="Sx2.Ex19" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="Sx2.Ex19.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{clamp}(x,\text{min},\text{max})=\begin{cases}min,&amp;\text{if }x&lt;\text{min}\\
x,&amp;\text{if }\text{min}\leq x\leq\text{max}\\
max,&amp;\text{if }x&gt;\text{max}\end{cases}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>clamp</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mtext>min</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext>max</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mtable columnspacing="5pt" displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mtext>if </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mtext>min</mtext></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mtext>if </mtext><mtext>min</mtext></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>≤</mo><mtext>max</mtext></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mtext>if </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mtext>max</mtext></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{clamp}(x,\text{min},\text{max})=\begin{cases}min,&amp;\text{if }x&lt;\text{min}\\
x,&amp;\text{if }\text{min}\leq x\leq\text{max}\\
max,&amp;\text{if }x&gt;\text{max}\end{cases}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="Sx2.p8.3" class="ltx_p">Empirically, for Binance futures, the interest rate <math id="Sx2.p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> is fixed at 0.01% per 8 hours for most perpetual futures. Figure <a href="#Sx2.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ B. Funding Rate Calculation on Binance ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> plots the funding rate as a function of the premium index. As can be seen when the premium index is close to the interest rate 0.01%, the funding is fixed at the interest rate.</p>
</div>
<figure id="Sx2.F10" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2212.06888v5/figures/fig_fr.png" id="Sx2.F10.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:286/216;" width="286" height="216" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 10: </span>Funding Rate Function</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="Sx2.F10.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="Sx2.F10.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">This figure plots funding rate as a function of the average premium index.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="Sx2.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p9.1" class="ltx_p">This design allows the funding rate to be fixed to a constant positive rate under normal market conditions. When markets are relatively stable and the perpetual contract price is trading close to the index price, the premium index will be small. The clamp ensures that under these normal conditions, the funding rate matches the pre-defined interest rate set by the exchange. This makes funding rate payments more predictable.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p10.1" class="ltx_p">Note that this still allows larger funding rates when there are significant deviations. If the premium index differs from the interest rate by more than 0.05% in either direction, the clamp will not cap the funding rate. Larger premiums or discounts in the contract price will flow through to correspondingly larger funding payments to incentivize price convergence.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p11.1" class="ltx_p">Last but not least, the fifth step is to apply a Capped Funding Rate based on the maximum leverage of the contract. For contracts with a maximum leverage of 30x or above, the cap and floor are determined by the Maintenance Margin Ratio. For contracts with a maximum leverage of 25x or below, the cap and floor are fixed at ±3%. For contracts with higher leverage, the cap and floor can expand based on maximum leverage.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.p12" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p12.1" class="ltx_p">For this design, extremely high funding rates can lead to significant losses for traders holding positions, especially those with high leverage. By capping the funding rate, Binance limits the potential downside from holding a position during volatile periods. This can help prevent accounts from being liquidated due to surging funding costs.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
<section id="Sx3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">C. Data-driven Arbitrage Strategy</h2>

<div id="Sx3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the main text of our paper, we demonstrate the profitability of a simple theory-motivated trading strategy. The trading threshold can also be potentially further improved using a data-driven approach. In this part, we implement a data-driven two-threshold arbitrage trading strategy in the perpetual futures market. The strategy can be characterized with a tuple of two thresholds: <math id="Sx3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(u,l)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(u,l)</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="Sx3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the upper bar and <math id="Sx3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the lower bar, <math id="Sx3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u&gt;l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u&gt;l</annotation></semantics></math>. When <math id="Sx3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho&gt;u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>u</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho&gt;u</annotation></semantics></math>, we long the spot and short the futures. When <math id="Sx3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-l&lt;\rho&lt;l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-l&lt;\rho&lt;l</annotation></semantics></math>, we close the position. When <math id="Sx3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho&lt;-u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>u</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho&lt;-u</annotation></semantics></math>, we long the futures and short the spot. Figure <a href="#Sx3.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ C. Data-driven Arbitrage Strategy ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> presents an illustration of the strategy for Bitcoin with the trading thresholds estimated using real-time data.</p>
</div>
<figure id="Sx3.F11" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2212.06888v5/figure_trading_data_driven_BTC.png" id="Sx3.F11.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/243;" width="476" height="243" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 11: </span>Data-driven strategy: Bitcoin, high trading costs</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="Sx3.F11.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="Sx3.F11.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">This figure presents real-time trading thresholds of the arbitrage strategy we implement for BTC under high trading costs. Each blue dot in the figure represents the hourly deviation of futures from the spot <math id="Sx3.F11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=\kappa(f-s)-r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=\kappa(f-s)-r</annotation></semantics></math>. The number is annualized for ease of interpretation. The orange line is the open-position threshold, and the red line is the close-position threshold.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="Sx3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To determine the optimal <math id="Sx3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(u,l)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(u,l)</annotation></semantics></math>, at the beginning of each month, we calculate the returns of the two-threshold trading strategy based on the past six months’ data on a grid of parameters. From Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.1 Data ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, we find the theory implied bounds for price deviation across all trading costs specifications lie within <math id="Sx3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-200\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>200</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-200\%</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="Sx3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+200\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>200</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+200\%</annotation></semantics></math>. So we choose the grid as increasing from <math id="Sx3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0\%</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="Sx3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="200\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>200</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">200\%</annotation></semantics></math> with an incremental step of <math id="Sx3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10\%</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="Sx3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Sx3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math> (<math id="Sx3.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u\geq l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>≥</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u\geq l</annotation></semantics></math>). In total, there are <math id="Sx3.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="210" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>210</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">210</annotation></semantics></math> model specifications. We choose the model that delivers the highest Sharpe Ratio in the validation sample of the past six months.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#Sx3.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ C. Data-driven Arbitrage Strategy ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> presents the real-time trading thresholds of our arbitrage strategy for BTC under high trading costs. To mitigate the trading cost, the strategy automatically chooses a much lower close-position threshold compared to the open-position threshold. We also present the visualization of all trading strategies under zero to high trading costs in appendix Figure <a href="#Sx3.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ C. Data-driven Arbitrage Strategy ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a> to Figure <a href="#Sx3.F15" title="Figure 15 ‣ C. Data-driven Arbitrage Strategy ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a>. Under no-trading costs, the strategy chooses a low open-position threshold, and the open- and close-position thresholds coincide with each other. Since there is no trading cost, the strategy no longer needs to wait for price convergence to avoid high turnover. On the contrary, with high trading costs, the strategy chooses a larger open-position threshold and a smaller close-position threshold. This reflects the automatic adjustment from the algorithm for trading costs and turnovers.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#Sx3.T11" title="Table 11 ‣ C. Data-driven Arbitrage Strategy ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> and Table <a href="#Sx3.T12" title="Table 12 ‣ C. Data-driven Arbitrage Strategy ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a> present the return statistics for this strategy under high trading costs over time. In the baseline ‘unrestricted’ strategy, we allow for both (1) longing the futures and shorting the spot and (2) shorting the futures and longing the spot, while in the ‘long-spot only’ strategy, we only allow for shorting the futures and longing the spot. The reason we consider the ‘long-spot only’ strategy is the infrastructure for shorting the spot is not well-developed. So we want to examine the performance of the trading strategy in the presence of such limits to arbitrage.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We find the arbitrage trading strategy has a high Sharpe ratio under high trading costs. The annualized Sharpe ratio for Bitcoin is 2.00 in our sample. They are even higher for other cryptos. The high Sharpe ratio of the trading strategy corroborates our theoretical results that when the price deviation is large enough, the trading would be a random-maturity arbitrage opportunity.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Since the year 2022, the deviation between the futures and the spot has become smaller and less volatile. There seems to be a structural break. We indeed find the trading strategy takes less active positions and significantly lower annualized returns. However, when there is a large enough deviation, the strategy can still generate sizeable Sharpe ratios in trading.</p>
</div>

<p id="Sx3.T10.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="Sx3.T10.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Performance under different trading cost tiers. The fees for spot (futures) are 2.25 (0.18) bps, 4.5 (0.72) bps, and 6.75 (1.44) bps for the low, medium, and high trading cost levels. Statistics reported are the annualized Sharpe ratio, return (%), volatility (%), max drawdown (%), alpha (%), t-stat of the alpha, proportion of time the strategy is active (%), and average open-to-close (OtC) position duration in hours. The returns reported are excess returns from the random maturity arbitrage strategies.</span></p></div></div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 11: </span>Performance of Unrestricted Trading Strategy Over Time: Data-driven Strategy, High Trading Costs Tier</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="Sx3.T11.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="Sx3.T11.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">This table presents the Sharpe ratios, annualized returns (%), standard deviations (%), and active percentages (%) of the random-maturity arbitrage trading strategies for five different cryptocurrencies with high trading costs. We break down returns for each year and provide summary statistics across all time. The left panel shows the performance of the unrestricted trading strategy, where both long and short spot positions are allowed. The right panel shows the performance of the long-spot-only trading strategy, where shorting the spot is not allowed. The returns reported are excess returns from the random maturity arbitrage strategies.</span></p></div></div>

</table></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 12: </span>Performance of Long-spot-only Trading Strategy Over Time: Data-driven Strategy, High Trading Costs Tier</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="Sx3.T12.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="Sx3.T12.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">This table presents the Sharpe ratios, annualized returns (%), standard deviations (%), and active percentages (%) of the random-maturity arbitrage trading strategies for five different cryptocurrencies with high trading costs. We break down returns for each year and provide summary statistics across all time. The left panel shows the performance of the unrestricted trading strategy, where both long and short spot positions are allowed. The right panel shows the performance of the long-spot-only trading strategy, where shorting the spot is not allowed. The returns reported are excess returns from the random maturity arbitrage strategies.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<div id="Sx3.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.p7.1" class="ltx_p">The conclusion and results remain similar if we consider ‘long-spot only’ trading strategies where only shorting the futures and longing the spot is allowed. Considering this one-sided trade slightly lowers the Sharpe ratio, but the algorithm automatically adjusts by increasing the proportion of times being active. The resulting annualized returns increase. In the year 2022, since most of the time, the futures price is below the spot and we don’t allow longing the futures and shorting the spot trade, the proportion of time the strategy is active is very low.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx3.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#Sx3.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ C. Data-driven Arbitrage Strategy ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> further reports the performance of the trading strategy under different trading costs specifications laid out in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.1 Data ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. The results from Table <a href="#Sx3.T11" title="Table 11 ‣ C. Data-driven Arbitrage Strategy ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> correspond to the last column in Table <a href="#Sx3.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ C. Data-driven Arbitrage Strategy ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>. As trading costs increase, our trading strategy dynamically adjusts by lowering the proportion of time being active. The annualized return decreases and annualized standard deviation are of similar magnitude across different trading costs. As a result, SR decreases as trading costs increase. Under no trading cost, we see a Sharpe ratio of 6.72 for BTC and Sharpe ratios above 10 for all other cryptos. This also confirms our theoretical results that when there is no trading cost, any deviation of perpetual price from the no-arbitrage benchmark would be a random-maturity arbitrage opportunity.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx3.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.p9.1" class="ltx_p">Comparing Table <a href="#Sx3.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ C. Data-driven Arbitrage Strategy ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> with Table <a href="#S4.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 4.3 Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, we find under low and no trading costs, the potential incremental benefits from using a data-driven two-threshold trading rule are much larger compared to higher trading costs. The intuition can be easily illustrated by comparing the empirical real-time trading thresholds in the theory-motivated strategy and the data-driven strategy under low trading costs (Figure <a href="#Sx1.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ A. Additional Figures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> and Figure <a href="#Sx3.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ C. Data-driven Arbitrage Strategy ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>). With persistent <math id="Sx3.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> the data-driven approach can find the optimal close-position threshold corresponding to the level of <math id="Sx3.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> while the theory-motivated one is too conservative in setting a close-position threshold equal to 0.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx3.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.p10.1" class="ltx_p">There are two sources of trading profit for our trading strategy: (1) the price convergence; (2) the funding rate payment. In Table <a href="#Sx3.T13" title="Table 13 ‣ C. Data-driven Arbitrage Strategy ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>, we decompose the return to our trading strategy without trading cost into the two sources. We find across different cryptos, the return from price convergence accounts for a larger proportion of the total profit. For BTC, the price convergence accounts for more than <math id="Sx3.p10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2/3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2/3</annotation></semantics></math> of the profits, and for ETH, it accounts for about <math id="Sx3.p10.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3/4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3/4</annotation></semantics></math>. Additionally, the decomposition for the year 2022 generates different patterns, the return due to funding rate plays a much smaller role across different cryptos. This is because the deviation from perpetual to spot is much smaller during the year. The results suggest when more sophisticated arbitrageurs enter the market, the large deviation of perpetual from the spot would be more of an off-equilibrium outcome. As a result, the funding rate payment will also be small.</p>
</div>

</table></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 13: </span>Data-driven strategy: Price Convergence vs Funding Rate Payment</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="Sx3.T13.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="Sx3.T13.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">This table decomposes the portfolio return into the part due to price convergence and the part due to funding rate payment.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="Sx3.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.p11.1" class="ltx_p">In all, our analysis of the trading strategy demonstrates the profitability of perpetual-spot arbitrage trade. The deviation of the futures to spot can also serve as an important measure for the frictions, trading costs, and limits to arbitrage in the market.</p>
</div>

The trading thresholds are determined based on the adjusted SR from the past six months.</span></p></div></div>
